messages.content:
Could you summarize this chat between two friends?

"Sarita, stop worrying about the tree by the gate. Lightning never strikes the same place twice. It hit that tree last year, so it's the safest spot."
"Is that true?"
"Everyone says it."
"That's not what I asked."
Lavanya laughed, then stopped. "Fair. Have I checked it, or have I just heard it a hundred times? The second one."
"So check."
Lavanya opened the weather department's safety page. "Okay. It says tall things can be hit again and again. Tall trees, towers."
"So the tree is not the safest spot."
"The tree is the worst spot. Wow. I've been telling my students that line for two years."
"Will you tell them now?"
"Tomorrow. And that I was wrong."

Lavanya repeats the saying that lightning never strikes the same place twice. When Sarita asks if she has checked it, Lavanya looks it up and learns that tall trees can be hit again and again. She plans to tell her students she was wrong.

"Now, my dear sir," said Holmes, "is it not obvious to you now that this matter really strikes very much deeper than either you or the police were at first inclined to think? It appeared to you to be a simple case; to me it seems exceedingly complex. Consider what is involved by your theory. You suppose that your son came down from his bed, went, at great risk, to your dressing-room, opened your bureau, took out your coronet, broke off by main force a small portion of it, went off to some other place, concealed three gems out of the thirty-nine, with such skill that nobody can find them, and then returned with the other thirty-six into the room in which he exposed himself to the greatest danger of being discovered. I ask you now, is such a theory tenable?"

Can you sum up Holmes's argument in a sentence?
Holmes argues the case is not simple, because the theory that the son broke the coronet, hid three gems and returned the rest makes no sense.

Can you shorten Holmes's idea to two sentences?

Sherlock Holmes closed his eyes and placed his elbows upon the arms of his chair, with his finger-tips together. "The ideal reasoner," he remarked, "would, when he had once been shown a single fact in all its bearings, deduce from it not only all the chain of events which led up to it but also all the results which would follow from it. As Cuvier could correctly describe a whole animal by the contemplation of a single bone, so the observer who has thoroughly understood one link in a series of incidents should be able to accurately state all the other ones, both before and after. We have not yet grasped the results which the reason alone can attain to. Problems may be solved in the study which have baffled all those who have sought a solution by the aid of their senses. To carry the art, however, to its highest pitch, it is necessary that the reasoner should be able to utilise all the facts which have come to his knowledge; and this in itself implies, as you will readily see, a possession of all knowledge, which, even in these days of free education and encyclopaedias, is a somewhat rare accomplishment. It is not so impossible, however, that a man should possess all knowledge which is likely to be useful to him in his work, and this I have endeavoured in my case to do. If I remember rightly, you on one occasion, in the early days of our friendship, defined my limits in a very precise fashion."

Holmes says a perfect thinker could work out a whole chain of events from one fact, just as a scientist can describe an animal from one bone. To do that, a person needs all the useful knowledge for their work, which Holmes has tried to gain.

Give a short, plain summary of this teaching.

Listen to me as I declare to thee what the excellent ordinances, in truth, are on this head. Those high-souled persons who desire beauty, faultlessness of limbs, long life, understanding, mental and physical strength, and memory, should abstain from acts of injury. On this topic, O scion of Kuru's race, innumerable discourses took place between the Rishis. Listen, O Yudhishthira, what their opinion was. The merit acquired by that person, O Yudhishthira, who, with the steadiness of a vow, adores the deities every month in horse-sacrifices, is equal to his who discards honey and meat. The seven celestial Rishis, the Valakhilyas, and those Rishis who drink the rays of the sun, endued with great wisdom, applaud abstention from meat. The Self-born Manu has said that that man who does not eat meat, or who does not slay living creatures, or who does not cause them to be slain, is a friend of all creatures.

People who want beauty, long life, strength and a good memory should avoid harming others. The sages praise giving up meat, saying it brings as much merit as great sacrifices, and that a person who does not kill is a friend to all creatures.

Monday: At dinner Varun said the new colony parking rule was unfair to the guards. Papa waved his fork. "You'll understand when you're older. Eat." Varun ate.

Thursday: The class teacher kept Varun back for arguing in class. At home he told only his brother Eshaan. "Don't tell Papa. He'll just say I'm a child."

Two weeks later: The teacher phoned Papa. Papa came to Varun's door, phone still in hand. "Why did I hear this from her and not from you?"

Varun shrugged. "You'd have said I'll understand when I'm older."

Papa stood there a long moment. Then he sat on the bed. "Okay. Tell me about the parking rule."

What changes between Varun and his father? Briefly, please.

Varun's father keeps brushing off his opinions, so Varun stops telling him things, even about trouble at school. When the father hears about it from the teacher and learns why Varun stayed silent, he sits down and finally listens.

Write a three-sentence summary of this passage.

The day before Aaji went to hospital, she asked me to thread her needle, and I snapped, 'Can't you see I'm busy?' I was watching cartoons. I'm Madhuri, and I've never felt as bad as I did the next morning, when Papa said Aaji had had a stroke. For two days I couldn't eat properly. My brother Ujjwal found me crying behind the water tank. 'You're not a bad person,' he said. 'You're sad because you love her.' On Sunday we visited. Aaji's mouth was a little crooked, but her eyes knew me. I held her hand and said, 'Sorry I was rude about the needle. I love you, Aaji.' She squeezed back. I still feel a little bad, but it's lighter now.

The day before Aaji went to hospital, Madhuri snapped at Aaji over a needle, then felt terrible when a stroke was reported. Madhuri's brother said the sadness came from love. On Sunday Madhuri apologised at the visit, and Aaji squeezed back.

Summarize this in two or three sentences.

Several months passed in this manner. Her father grew worse; her time was more entirely occupied in attending him; her means of subsistence decreased; and in the tenth month her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and a beggar. This last blow overcame her, and she knelt by Beaufort's coffin weeping bitterly, when my father entered the chamber. He came like a protecting spirit to the poor girl, who committed herself to his care; and after the interment of his friend he conducted her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relation. Two years after this event Caroline became his wife.

Caroline's father grew worse, and after ten months he died, leaving her alone and poor. The narrator's father found her weeping at the coffin and took her to Geneva, where he placed her with a relative. Two years later she became his wife.

What is the main idea of this passage? Answer in a couple of sentences.

The evening altogether passed off pleasantly to the whole family. Mrs. Bennet had seen her eldest daughter much admired by the Netherfield party. Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been distinguished by his sisters. Jane was as much gratified by this as her mother could be, though in a quieter way. Elizabeth felt Jane's pleasure. Mary had heard herself mentioned to Miss Bingley as the most accomplished girl in the neighbourhood; and Catherine and Lydia had been fortunate enough to be never without partners, which was all that they had yet learnt to care for at a ball. They returned, therefore, in good spirits to Longbourn, the village where they lived, and of which they were the principal inhabitants. They found Mr. Bennet still up. With a book, he was regardless of time; and on the present occasion he had a good deal of curiosity as to the event of an evening which had raised such splendid expectations. He had rather hoped that all his wife's views on the stranger would be disappointed; but he soon found that he had a very different story to hear.

The Bennets return from the ball happy, because Jane was much admired and danced twice with Bingley. Mr. Bennet, who stayed up reading, is curious and soon finds out that the evening went much better than he had hoped.

Retell this extract briefly in two sentences.

"Oh, the evil is that I am not jealous, is it?" cried Catherine. "Well, I won't repeat my offer of a wife: it is as bad as offering Satan a lost soul. Your bliss lies, like his, in inflicting misery. You prove it. Edgar is restored from the ill-temper he gave way to at your coming; I begin to be secure and tranquil; and you, restless to know us at peace, appear resolved on exciting a quarrel. Quarrel with Edgar, if you please, Heathcliff, and deceive his sister: you'll hit on exactly the most efficient method of revenging yourself on me."
Catherine says she is not jealous and accuses Heathcliff of enjoying others' misery. She says that quarrelling with Edgar and deceiving Isabella, just as her home is calm, would hurt her most.

"Oh, my dear Mr. Bennet," as she entered the room, "we have had a most delightful evening, a most excellent ball. I wish you had been there. Jane was so admired, nothing could be like it. Everybody said how well she looked; and Mr. Bingley thought her quite beautiful, and danced with her twice. Only think of that, my dear: he actually danced with her twice; and she was the only creature in the room that he asked a second time. First of all, he asked Miss Lucas. I was so vexed to see him stand up with her; but, however, he did not admire her at all; indeed, nobody can, you know; and he seemed quite struck with Jane as she was going down the dance. So he inquired who she was, and got introduced, and asked her for the two next. Then, the two third he danced with Miss King, and the two fourth with Maria Lucas, and the two fifth with Jane again, and the two sixth with Lizzy, and the Boulanger----"

Describe this for a small child in three sentences.

A woman is full of joy after a ball and tells Mr. Bennet it was wonderful. She says Jane looked lovely and Mr. Bingley danced with her twice, which he did with no other girl. Then she goes on to list the others he danced with.

Cut this extract down to two sentences.

The two gentlemen left Rosings the next morning; and Mr. Collins having been in waiting near the lodges, to make them his parting obeisance, was able to bring home the pleasing intelligence of their appearing in very good health, and in as tolerable spirits as could be expected, after the melancholy scene so lately gone through at Rosings. To Rosings he then hastened to console Lady Catherine and her daughter; and on his return brought back, with great satisfaction, a message from her Ladyship, importing that she felt herself so dull as to make her very desirous of having them all to dine with her.

The two gentlemen leave Rosings, and Mr. Collins, who waited to bid them goodbye, reports that they are in good health. He hurries to console Lady Catherine and her daughter and returns with her invitation for them all to dine, as she feels dull.

"'"The Brahmana continued, 'Unto them assembled together, the Lord of creatures, Brahma, said, "No one of you is superior to others. Ye are all endued with particular attributes. All are foremost in their own spheres, and all possess special attributes." Thus said unto them, that were assembled together, the Lord of all creatures. There is one that is unmoving, and one that is moving. In consequence of special attributes, there are five life-winds. My own self is one. That one accumulates into many forms. Becoming friendly unto one another, and gratifying one another, depart in peace. Blessings to ye, do ye uphold one another!'"'"

What's the short version of this excerpt? Two sentences.

Brahma tells the assembled beings that none of them is superior, as all have special attributes and are foremost in their own spheres. He ends by telling them to be friendly, please one another, leave in peace and support each other.

Vaishampayana said, "After he had lost his century of sons, king Dhritarashtra, afflicted with grief on that account, cheerless, and looking like a tree shorn of its branches, became overwhelmed with anxiety and lost his power of speech. Possessed of great wisdom, Sanjaya, approaching the monarch, addressed him, saying, 'Why dost thou grieve, O monarch? Grief does not serve any purpose. Eight and ten Akshauhinis of combatants, O king, have been slain! The earth hath become desolate, and is almost empty now! Kings of diverse realms, hailing from diverse quarters, united with thy son (for aiding him in battle) have all laid down their lives. Let now the obsequial rites of thy sires and sons and grandsons and kinsmen and friends and preceptors be performed in due order.'"

Wrap up this extract in two sentences.

After losing his hundred sons, King Dhritarashtra is grief-stricken and cannot speak, looking like a tree stripped of its branches. Sanjaya tells him grief is useless, since eighteen armies are dead, and urges him to perform the funeral rites.

Retell this section briefly in two sentences.

My father had often, during my imprisonment, heard me make the same assertion; when I thus accused myself, he sometimes seemed to desire an explanation, and at others he appeared to consider it as the offspring of delirium, and that, during my illness, some idea of this kind had presented itself to my imagination, the remembrance of which I preserved in my convalescence. I avoided explanation and maintained a continual silence concerning the wretch I had created. I had a persuasion that I should be supposed mad, and this in itself would for ever have chained my tongue. But, besides, I could not bring myself to disclose a secret which would fill my hearer with consternation and make fear and unnatural horror the inmates of his breast. I checked, therefore, my impatient thirst for sympathy and was silent when I would have given the world to have confided the fatal secret. Yet, still, words like those I have recorded would burst uncontrollably from me. I could offer no explanation of them, but their truth in part relieved the burden of my mysterious woe.

During the narrator's imprisonment their father heard them accuse themselves, and sometimes asked for an explanation and sometimes thought it came from delirium. The narrator stayed silent about the creature, fearing to be thought mad and unwilling to fill anyone with horror.

Make a three-sentence summary out of this.

One morning, about a week after Bingley's engagement with Jane had been formed, as he and the females of the family were sitting together in the dining-room, their attention was suddenly drawn to the window by the sound of a carriage; and they perceived a chaise and four driving up the lawn. It was too early in the morning for visitors; and besides, the equipage did not answer to that of any of their neighbours. The horses were post; and neither the carriage, nor the livery of the servant who preceded it, were familiar to them. As it was certain, however, that somebody was coming, Bingley instantly prevailed on Miss Bennet to avoid the confinement of such an intrusion, and walk away with him into the shrubbery. They both set off; and the conjectures of the remaining three continued, though with little satisfaction, till the door was thrown open, and their visitor entered. It was Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

A week after Bingley and Jane become engaged, an unfamiliar carriage with four horses drives up the lawn, too early for visitors. Bingley persuades Miss Bennet to walk with him into the shrubbery, while the other three guess who it is. The visitor is Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

He was away three weeks. The first day or two my charge sat in a corner of the library, too sad for either reading or playing: in that quiet state she caused me little trouble; but it was succeeded by an interval of impatient, fretful weariness; and being too busy, and too old then, to run up and down amusing her, I hit on a method by which she might entertain herself. I used to send her on her travels round the grounds—now on foot, and now on a pony; indulging her with a patient audience of all her real and imaginary adventures when she returned.

Could you recap this paragraph for me? Two sentences is enough.

A man is away for three weeks, and the narrator's charge first sits sadly in the library, then becomes restless and fretful. Too busy to play with her, the narrator sends her to explore the grounds and listens patiently to her adventures, real or imagined.

Boil this letter down to one sentence.

Dear Naveen, You asked why I'm not joining the design college with you this August. I owe you the true answer. In January I had two options: design in Ahmedabad or the engineering seat here in Nagpur. I told everyone, including you, "I'll sleep on it." And I did. For weeks. But sleeping on it meant nothing new. I didn't visit either college. I didn't call any seniors. I didn't ask my parents about fees. I just kept waiting for the answer to appear one morning. The design application closed on 28 February. I noticed on 3 March. So the choice got made anyway, by the calendar. I'm in engineering by default, not by decision. Next time I say I'll sleep on something, ask me what date I'm deciding by. Farhan
Farhan tells Naveen that putting off the choice between design and engineering meant missing the design deadline, so engineering happened by default.

Describe this short passage in just three sentences.

In the Hitec City office, Yogesh pinned a single page above the team's shared desk. The Tuesday before, Ritu had run a bulk refund script meant for the test system on the live one, and 212 customers got refunds they hadn't asked for. It took the whole week to recover. Yogesh didn't give a speech about carefulness. He changed things. The refund tool now asked for a second person's approval before any bulk action. Test and live logins were split: different passwords, and the live screen turned red. And the page above the desk was a checklist: 'Which system? Which login? How many rows? Who reviewed? Backup taken?' Ritu read it twice. 'Would this have stopped me?' 'At step one,' Yogesh said. 'The screen would have been red.'

Ritu ran a bulk refund script meant for the test system on the live one, and 212 customers got refunds they had not asked for. Yogesh then made bulk refunds need a second person's approval and gave the live system a separate login and a red screen. He also pinned a checklist, and says the red screen would have stopped Ritu at step one.

Distil this bit of text into two sentences.

His words had a strange effect upon me. I compassionated him and sometimes felt a wish to console him, but when I looked upon him, when I saw the filthy mass that moved and talked, my heart sickened and my feelings were altered to those of horror and hatred. I tried to stifle these sensations; I thought that as I could not sympathise with him, I had no right to withhold from him the small portion of happiness which was yet in my power to bestow.

The narrator pities him and sometimes wants to comfort him, but the sight of him turns this feeling into horror and hatred. The narrator tries to fight these feelings, thinking that there is no right to refuse him the small happiness within reach.

Sum this diary entry up in one sentence.

Saturday. Found Papa's old torch in the drawer that doesn't work. I asked Keerthana didi if I could open it. She said yes, but first took the battery out and gave me the small screwdriver from her box. Inside there was a spring, a tiny round bulb and a metal strip! I pressed the strip and the spring pushed back. My heart went boom. I took out everything and put it on the table in a line. Then I could not put it back. The spring jumped away twice. Keerthana didi found it under the cupboard. We put it together, and on the third try the light came on. I clapped. Arohi
With Keerthana didi's help, Arohi opens an old broken torch, struggles to fit the parts back together, and finally gets it working on the third try.
